adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The train pulled out of the station a little before dawn, and for a long while the only thing visible through the window was the dark outline of the hills. Somewhere beyond the ridge a river wound its way north, though it was still too early to see the water. The woman in the next seat unwrapped a small loaf of bread and offered half of it to the boy beside her. He took it without a word and watched the fields slide past, one after another, each one greyer than the last. By the time the sun came up the clouds had broken into thin ribbons and the whole valley was full of a pale, steady light.

The old man farther down the carriage had begun to talk about the winter he once spent in the mountains, and the story went on and on, circling the same few details without ever reaching an end. He described a cabin with a leaking roof, a stove that would not draw, and a dog that followed him through the snow for three days before it turned back at the treeline. Nobody interrupted him. The boy listened with his chin propped on his hand, and the woman beside him pretended to read, though her page never turned.

At the second stop a family climbed aboard carrying baskets that smelled of onions and wet wool, and for a while the carriage was loud with greetings in a language that none of the passengers around them understood. The conductor came through twice, punched their tickets, and announced that the next station would be the last one before the border. Outside, a flock of birds lifted from a frozen pond and scattered across the sky in a long, ragged line.

By noon the light had gone flat and grey again, and the hills had softened into a single wide plain with hardly a tree on it. The old man fell asleep with his mouth open, and the story he had been telling simply stopped, as if it had never had an ending at all. The boy pressed his forehead to the cold glass and watched the wires rise and fall along the track, rise and fall, all the way to the horizon, until the motion and the humming of the wheels put him to sleep as well. Nobody on the train knew what waited on the other side of the border, and perhaps that was the point of the journey: to arrive somewhere without already knowing what it would look like.
